# below is read from it, so each one is per-INSTANCE configuration -- two

# beside each name is the shipped default; it is the same value the template

P = doc.get("params") or {}


def _knob(key, default):
    # A knob explicitly set to NULL is "not configured", not a crash: an
    # operator who blanks a line in a config means the default. WHITESPACE is
    # decided one level down, by the accessor, because the two classes want
    # opposite things: `_int` falls back on a blank string (there is no number
    # in it), while `_str` keeps it -- so a blanked `canon_judge` is not the
    # shipped "1", it is a value that is not "1", and the ask is off. That is
    # the reading an operator who blanks the line means.
    v = P.get(key, default)
    return default if v is None else v


def _int(key, default):
    v = _knob(key, default)
    if isinstance(v, str) and not v.strip():
        return default
    return int(v)


def _str(key, default):
    v = _knob(key, default)
    return "" if v is None else str(v)

def parse_model_json(text):
    """Read a model answer that may be fenced (```json ... ```) or wrapped in a
    sentence. Same lesson as the extraction lane: the first live run of a new llm
    cell is where the fence shows up, and a lane that only accepts bare JSON turns
    that into a silent nightly no-op."""
    t = (text or "").strip()
    if t.startswith("```"):
        t = t.split("\n", 1)[1] if "\n" in t else t[3:]
        if t.rstrip().endswith("```"):
            t = t.rstrip()[:-3]
    try:
        return json.loads(t)
    except Exception:
        pass
    a, b = t.find("{"), t.rfind("}")
    if a >= 0 and b > a:
        try:
            return json.loads(t[a:b + 1])
        except Exception:
            return None
    return None


def belief_id(holder, statement):
    return hashlib.sha256(("|".join([str(holder), str(statement)])).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]


# --------------------------------------------------- PREDICATE CORE LIST (P1)
# Curated seed vocabulary of the extraction lane (rulings Q1/Q2/Q4). Byte mirror
# of templates/memory-hive/predicate-core.json -- THAT file is the
# authority, this is the copy a script can carry (a script cannot import), and
# crates/meclaw-cells/tests/extract_canonicalization.rs compares the RENDERED
# prompt against it, so the two cannot drift apart unnoticed.
#   single = one value at a time; a later value replaces the earlier one, and
#            this is where the version chain fires.
#   multi  = the axis ENUMERATES; values coexist and a new one ends nothing
#            (ruling Q4: supersession is not derived on such an axis).
# Keep the two anchor comments: P2 lifts this block for the chain derivation.
CORE_SINGLE = ["born_on", "diet", "favorite_color", "favorite_food", "favorite_music",
               "job_title", "lives_in", "partner_of", "preferred_language", "pronouns",
               "relationship_status", "timezone", "works_at"]
CORE_MULTI = ["allergic_to", "dislikes", "friend_of", "has_child", "has_parent",
              "has_pet", "has_sibling", "likes", "lived_in", "member_of", "owns",
              "skilled_in", "speaks_language", "studied_at", "visited", "worked_at"]
# -------------------------------------------------- /PREDICATE CORE LIST (P1)


def build_chains(rows):
    """Group facts into (CANONICAL subject, CANONICAL predicate) version chains.

    BOTH halves of the key are store-owned identities, never written spellings
    (0.2.0 P2 ruling Q3 for the relation, P4 ruling Q5 for the entity):
    `Lieblingseditor` and `favorite_editor` are one relation, `user` and
    `user:alex` are one person, and on separate axes the version chain simply
    never fires -- which is the measured defect (chain-fire rate 5 percent) this
    wave exists for.

    The axis is the RETRIEVAL grouping and nothing more (statement identity W2,
    ruling Q1): what supersedes what is decided one level down, on the statement
    `(canonical_subject, canonical_predicate, canonical_claim)`. Recall stays
    coarse, correctness moves down.

    The order is the ruling, not an implementation detail: without the full
    tie-break two runs could disagree on which fact is current.
    """
    axes = {}
    for r in rows:
        axes.setdefault((subject_key(r), axis_key(r)), []).append(r)
    for key in axes:
        axes[key].sort(key=lambda f: (f.get("valid_from") or "",
                                      f.get("recorded_at") or "",
                                      f.get("id") or ""))
    return axes


def axis_key(fact):
    """The IDENTITY of a fact's relation -- the store-owned canonical predicate.

    The written spelling is the fallback, for two honest cases: a row from before
    the migration, and a store that carries no canonical binding at all. Falling
    back keeps such a row on an axis of its own instead of collapsing every one of
    them into a single None bucket.
    """
    return fact.get("canonical_predicate") or fact.get("predicate")


def subject_key(fact):
    """The IDENTITY of the entity a fact is about -- the store-owned canonical
    subject (0.2.0 P4, ruling Q5).

    Same shape and same fallback as `axis_key` one dimension over: `user` and
    `user:alex` are the same person exactly when the store says so, and a row
    written before the migration keeps an axis of its own rather than collapsing
    into a single None bucket.
    """
    return fact.get("canonical_subject") or fact.get("subject")


def statement_key(fact):
    """The IDENTITY of what a fact SAYS -- the store-owned canonical claim
    (statement identity W2, ruling Q1).

    The third dimension, and the one that turns the axis from the supersession
    unit into a retrieval grouping: a third plan cannot end the first two,
    because three plans are three statements rather than three versions of one.

    Same shape and same fallback as the other two dimensions, and the fallback
    matters most here -- a row written before the migration keeps a statement of
    its own instead of joining every other unmigrated row in one None bucket,
    where a single later fact would end all of them at once.

    Byte identity of the claim is the day-one canonical value: `canonical_claim`
    is derived by the generic binding in `params.canonical` and no alias exists
    until the judged claim aliases ship, so two wordings of one value are two
    statements for now. The direction of that error is the harmless one -- the
    axis shows both instead of ending one.
    """
    return fact.get("canonical_claim") or fact.get("claim")


def different_sessions(a, b):
    """Did these two facts arrive in two DIFFERENT conversations? (W1, ruling Q3)

    `session_id` is stamped on the fact row at write time, from the episode the
    fact was extracted from. The store has no joins, and a read path that pays a
    round trip per axis to learn the origin would pay it on every recall.

    Both ids must be present and they must differ: an unknown origin is not
    evidence of a different one. A row written before the column existed
    therefore proves nothing, which is the conservative direction and the one
    the seeded list stands in front of.
    """
    left = str(a.get("session_id") or "")
    right = str(b.get("session_id") or "")
    return bool(left) and bool(right) and left != right


def axis_is_multivalued(chain, judged=None):
    """Does this axis ENUMERATE instead of changing state? (O-3 + rulings Q4/Q3)

    THREE sources with a fixed precedence, and the order is the ruling (Q3):

    1. SEEDED (0.2.0 P2, the #13 interim) -- the AUTHORITY. The canonical
       predicate stands on one of the two curated lists, and that answers the
       question in both directions. A store may not even hold a judged verdict
       for such a relation: the nightly round refuses to write one, so this arm
       and the write path state one precedence rather than two.
    2. JUDGED (statement identity W5, ruling Q3 option C) -- one persisted,
       attributed verdict per canonical predicate, produced by the nightly round
       and passed in by the caller. `single` and `multi` are the only two words
       that mean anything; anything else falls through, because the map comes
       from a store column and a column can carry anything.
    3. LEARNED, GUARDED BY THE SESSION (statement identity W1, ruling Q3): two
       facts of the axis started at the same instant AND arrived in two
       DIFFERENT sessions. Monotone -- once an axis has coexisted across two
       conversations it counts as an enumeration from then on.

    Since W2 (ruling Q1) this is NOT the supersession decider any more. It says
    nothing about what ends what; it is a PRESENTATION tie-breaker, and the only
    question it answers is whether an axis has a "current value" to collapse a
    hit onto at all. An enumeration has none by definition, so every hit of one
    stays its own answer.

    That demotion is what makes a wrong verdict harmless, which is exactly what
    ruling Q3 predicted once the value became part of the identity: it can fail
    to mark an outdated value, it can no longer silently end a true one -- and it
    is why a JUDGED layer may be added here at all.

    Every list and every key is the CANONICAL predicate, which is why
    canonicalisation had to land first: cardinality is a property of the
    relation, not of the spelling someone happened to use.
    """
    key = str(axis_key(chain[0])) if chain else ""
    if key in CORE_MULTI:
        return True
    if key in CORE_SINGLE:
        return False
    verdict = (judged or {}).get(key)
    if verdict in ("single", "multi"):
        return verdict == "multi"
    # The chain is sorted by valid_from, so the facts of one instant are
    # contiguous: walking backwards and stopping at the first different start
    # visits every same-instant pair once and nothing else.
    for i in range(1, len(chain)):
        for j in range(i - 1, -1, -1):
            if (chain[j].get("valid_from") or "") != (chain[i].get("valid_from") or ""):
                break
            if different_sessions(chain[i], chain[j]):
                return True
    return False


def next_reassertion(chain, i):
    """Index of the next STRICTLY later assertion of the SAME statement (W2).

    This is the whole of what ORDER may still decide (ruling Q1). Saying the same
    thing again months later is one statement with two assertions, so the older
    assertion becomes history and the newer one carries the value -- that half of
    the old arithmetic was never in doubt and is kept verbatim in effect.

    What is gone is the other half: a fact with a DIFFERENT claim is a different
    statement, and being later is not an argument about it. Peers starting at the
    same instant are not successors either, which is O-1 unchanged: what closes a
    span is the next assertion, not the next row.
    """
    start = chain[i].get("valid_from") or ""
    key = statement_key(chain[i])
    for j in range(i + 1, len(chain)):
        if (chain[j].get("valid_from") or "") > start and statement_key(chain[j]) == key:
            return j
    return None


def closure_is_explicit(fact):
    """Did a WRITER close this statement, or is the closure re-derivable? (W2)

    Ruling Q2 guard rail 2 -- "every closure carries its reason" -- as a column.
    Two things may close a statement now, and they behave differently under a
    re-derive: a later re-assertion of the same statement, which the chain finds
    again on every run, and an explicit judgement, which it cannot.

    So an explicit closure names its author and a re-derive leaves it alone,
    while an UNATTRIBUTED closure is exactly what the old axis arithmetic left
    behind and is withdrawn (ruling Q4). W2 writes nothing into this column; it
    is the slot the nightly judge fills.
    """
    return bool(str(fact.get("closure_source") or "").strip())


def span_end(chain, i):
    """End of chain[i]'s validity (W2, rulings Q1/Q2).

    Three sources, in this order:

    1. the fact's own `valid_until` -- a statement that says when it stops being
       true says it about itself, and nothing overrules that;
    2. the materialised closure -- across statement boundaries a span ends when
       an INVALIDATION says so, so this READS `expired_at` instead of deriving a
       second answer next to it. The read path and the stored column cannot
       disagree if only one of them decides;
    3. a strictly later assertion of the same statement, for the closure a dream
       run has not written down yet.

    What is deliberately absent is the axis arithmetic: a different value that
    happens to start later ends nothing. Until an explicit producer exists,
    nothing new closes automatically -- the bundle shows more coexistence, which
    is the harmless direction, and the currency marker (ruling Q6) already names
    what IS closed.
    """
    fact = chain[i]
    if fact.get("valid_until"):
        return fact["valid_until"]
    if fact.get("expired_at"):
        return fact["expired_at"]
    j = next_reassertion(chain, i)
    return (chain[j].get("valid_from") or None) if j is not None else None


def span_successor(chain, i):
    """Index of the fact that ENDED chain[i]'s span, or None (W2).

    The mirror of `span_end`, and it has to be a mirror or the projection and the
    rendered span would disagree about the same closure: an explicit
    `valid_until` names nobody, a materialised closure names the fact its
    `superseded_by` points at, and an unmaterialised re-assertion names the later
    assertion itself.

    A closure whose successor is not on the axis page returns None. That is not
    an error -- the statement is still closed, it just has no reachable name, and
    the currency marker renders exactly that case.
    """
    fact = chain[i]
    if fact.get("valid_until"):
        return None
    if fact.get("expired_at"):
        successor = str(fact.get("superseded_by") or "")
        for j in range(len(chain)):
            if successor and str(chain[j].get("id")) == successor:
                return j
        return None
    return next_reassertion(chain, i)


def chain_target(chain, i):
    """Follow the closures of chain[i] forward to the statement still standing.

    R4 says a superseded fact is a field on its successor rather than an answer
    of its own. W2 changes what "superseded" means and nothing else about that
    shape: it is CLOSED, not merely older than the newest row on the axis.

    A chain sorted by start cannot cycle, but `superseded_by` is data and could
    point backwards, so the walk carries its own visited set instead of trusting
    it. A closed statement whose successor is unreachable ends the walk at
    itself, which keeps it a candidate -- carrying its marker.
    """
    seen, cur = {i}, i
    while True:
        nxt = span_successor(chain, cur)
        if nxt is None or nxt in seen:
            return cur
        seen.add(nxt)
        cur = nxt


def derive_supersessions(axis_rows):
    """The (id, expired_at, superseded_by) triples a dream run materialises (R9,
    rebuilt for statement identity W2, rulings Q1/Q2/Q4).

    The AUTHORITATIVE state of the two closure columns, per fact, from two
    sources in this precedence and no third:

    1. an EXPLICIT closure that names its author -- not re-derivable, so it is
       carried through unchanged. It stands ABOVE the arithmetic on purpose: a
       judgement may be reverted by withdrawing it, never by out-computing it;
    2. a strictly later re-assertion of the SAME statement -- the only thing
       order may still decide.

    What used to be the first source is gone (GH #65): the fact's own
    `valid_until` was mirrored into `expired_at`. A declared end of validity is
    not an invalidation, and the mirror made the two columns mean one thing on
    write while every read treats them as two questions. The tier-0 foresight
    leg asks both -- `expired_at is_null` for "nobody closed this" and
    `valid_until or_null gt <recall instant>` for "the deadline has not passed"
    -- so a plan whose deadline lies in the FUTURE fell out of the bundle the
    first night after it was written, which is the opposite of what a foresight
    leg is for. The read-time comparison stays where it already was; only the
    write-time copy goes.

    `span_end` is untouched by the removal and that is what keeps the two paths
    in step: it reads `valid_until` FIRST and always did, so it answers exactly
    what it answered before while the cache column stops carrying a second copy
    of the same instant. The mirror also out-computed judgements, which is the
    one thing precedence 1 forbids: a fact carrying both a `valid_until` and an
    attributed closure had its `superseded_by` cleared and its `expired_at`
    overwritten every single night.

    Everything else is (None, None), and that is the point rather than a gap.
    The axis arithmetic is gone: before W2 a bucket axis like `planned_activity`
    (71 values on one axis) counted as one functional relation, so a dream run
    would have closed 73 percent of all foresight facts across the eight
    benchmark stores the moment W1 thawed the axes. Nothing new closes now until
    a judgement says so, which is the harmless direction of error.

    Emitting a row for EVERY fact is what makes ruling Q4's withdrawal work: the
    caller writes only the differences, so an unattributed closure the old rule
    left behind is cleared back to NULL and an attributed one is a no-op. The
    axis order is total so two runs emit the same sequence.

    The asymmetry against `span_end` is deliberate and is the whole attribution
    argument in one line: READING a closure needs no author (it is the store's
    own verdict), WITHDRAWING one does.
    """
    axes = build_chains(axis_rows)
    order = sorted(axes, key=lambda k: (k[0] is None, k[0] or "",
                                        k[1] is None, k[1] or ""))
    out = []
    for key in order:
        chain = axes[key]
        for i, f in enumerate(chain):
            if closure_is_explicit(f):
                out.append((f.get("id"), f.get("expired_at") or None,
                            f.get("superseded_by") or None))
            else:
                j = next_reassertion(chain, i)
                out.append((f.get("id"),
                            chain[j].get("valid_from") or None if j is not None else None,
                            chain[j].get("id") if j is not None else None))
    return out


def extract_cutoff():
    """The lower bound of the closure review, derived from `delta_to` (W4).

    `delta_to` is the only clock this lane has, so a re-run reads the same window
    back. A clock this cannot parse falls back to NO widening at all: the scan
    then reads exactly what it read before W4, the extractor's closure survives
    unreviewed, and the next parseable night reviews it. That is the safe
    direction -- the alternative would be an unbounded page.
    """
    try:
        t = datetime.datetime.strptime(delta_to[:19], "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
    except Exception:
        return ""
    return (t - datetime.timedelta(days=CANON_EXTRACT_LOOKBACK_DAYS)).strftime(
        "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")


def scratch_cutoff():
    """The lower bound of the night's scratch sweep, derived from `delta_to` (GH #375).

    Same clock and same fallback direction as `extract_cutoff`: `delta_to` is the
    only clock this lane has, so a replay of one window computes the same cutoff
    and deletes the same rows -- a sweep that read "now" would make two replays
    of one window differ. A clock this cannot parse sweeps NOTHING: an empty
    cutoff would otherwise render as an empty `where`, and a delete without a
    where is a table drop with extra steps.
    """
    try:
        t = datetime.datetime.strptime(delta_to[:19], "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
    except Exception:
        return ""
    return (t - datetime.timedelta(days=SCRATCH_TTL_DAYS)).strftime(
        "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")


def sweep_scratch():
    """Delete the lane state both bookkeeping tables have outlived (GH #375).

    Two ops, one per table, each bounded on `created_at`. Nothing durable is
    named here and nothing else ever will be: `scratch` and `recall_scratch` are
    transient by their own definition, every read of them is keyed on the run,
    request, batch or session that wrote them, and no lane reads a row it did not
    write itself. The No-Delete policy keeps standing where it belongs.

    It cannot break the close pass's meeting, and that is worth saying because it
    is the one read that looks like it might: the meeting orders `created_at
    desc` and takes the FIRST row it sees per kind, so it consumes the NEWEST
    parking -- the head of an ordering a cutoff only ever cuts the tail of.
    """
    cutoff = scratch_cutoff()
    if not cutoff:
        return []
    return [store_op({"operation": "delete", "table": table,
                      "where": {"created_at": {"lt": cutoff}}}, "swept")
            for table in ("scratch", "recall_scratch")]


def canon_scan_where():
    """The scan reads the OPEN statements plus the recently closed ones.

    One column, one filter: `or_null` renders "expired_at >= cutoff OR expired_at
    is null". Everything the extractor did not close is filtered out again in
    `open_statement_axes` -- the widening buys the review, it does not change the
    two identity questions, which keep seeing live rows only.
    """
    cutoff = extract_cutoff()
    if not cutoff:
        return {"expired_at": {"is_null": True}}
    return {"expired_at": {"or_null": {"gte": cutoff}}}


def is_open(fact):
    """A row the store still holds as current."""
    return not str(fact.get("expired_at") or "")


def closed_read():
    """The rows a closure took OUT of the open set -- the identity questions' own
    read (GH #73).

    The defect it exists for: a statement written under spelling A is closed by a
    statement written under spelling B. That closure is the strongest evidence
    this memory ever produces that A and B are one relation, and it is exactly the
    event after which A stops being visible to the round -- the inventory and the
    entity context are built from OPEN rows, and A is open nowhere any more. The
    verdict that would unite the two chains is never proposed, in precisely the
    case where it is most certainly right.

    A READ of its own rather than a widening of the scan, and that is the half
    that is easy to get wrong. The scan already widens (`canon_scan_where`), but
    on `expired_at >= delta_to - lookback` -- and `expired_at` is when a statement
    stopped being TRUE, not when somebody wrote the closure down. A closure
    written last night about a change dated last spring is outside that window.
    The review lane needs that bound; this question needs a different one.

    So: most recently ENDED first, capped on ROWS. The order is the best guess
    this store can state about recency and the cap is what makes it safe when the
    guess is wrong -- the bound holds whatever the clock in the column says.
    """
    return store_op({"operation": "select", "table": "facts",
                     "columns": ["id", "subject", "canonical_subject", "predicate",
                                 "canonical_predicate", "claim", "expired_at",
                                 "superseded_by"],
                     "where": {"expired_at": {"is_null": False}},
                     "order_by": [{"col": "expired_at", "dir": "desc"},
                                  {"col": "id", "dir": "desc"}],
                     "limit": CANON_CLOSED_ROWS}, "canon-closed")


def closed_identities(rows):
    """The spellings and the claims the closed rows carry back into the two
    identity questions (GH #73).

    Same two maps the open scan builds, one page over: which subjects a spelling
    was used on (the predicate question) and what is known about a subject (the
    entity-pair question's context). They are MERGED at `canon-ask`, where both
    parked sides are in hand, and the merge is a plain union -- safe by
    construction, because the only spelling a union can add is one no open row
    carries, which is the spelling a closure across two spellings just took away.

    Bounded twice, and the order of the two bounds is the point: the rows arrive
    most recently ended first, so cutting the SPELLINGS first and reading the
    claims of the survivors second spends the context budget on the axes the
    question is actually about.
    """
    order, subjects_of = [], {}
    for r in rows:
        a, sub = axis_key(r), subject_key(r)
        if not (a and sub):
            continue
        a = str(a)
        if a not in subjects_of:
            subjects_of[a] = set()
            order.append(a)
        subjects_of[a].add(str(sub))
    keep = order[:CANON_MAX_CLOSED_AXES]
    predicates = {a: sorted(subjects_of[a])[:CANON_MAX_SUBJECTS_PER_PREDICATE] for a in keep}
    wanted = {s for a in keep for s in predicates[a]}
    context = {}
    for r in rows:
        sub, a = subject_key(r), axis_key(r)
        if not sub or str(sub) not in wanted or str(a or "") not in predicates:
            continue
        claim = str(r.get("claim") or "")
        if claim:
            context.setdefault(str(sub), set()).add(claim)
    return {"predicates": predicates,
            "context": {s: sorted(v)[:CANON_MAX_FACTS_PER_SIDE] for s, v in context.items()}}


def scan_read():
    """The round's own fact page: everything OPEN, plus the extractor closures
    this night has to review (W4).

    Unchanged since W4 -- lifted out of its phase into a helper because the
    identity read of GH #73 now runs in front of it and is the phase that emits
    it.
    """
    return store_op({"operation": "select", "table": "facts",
                     "columns": ["id", "subject", "canonical_subject", "predicate",
                                 "canonical_predicate", "claim", "canonical_claim",
                                 "fact_kind", "valid_from", "recorded_at", "expired_at",
                                 "closure_source"],
                     "where": canon_scan_where(),
                     "limit": AXIS_LIMIT}, "canon-scan")


def judged_verdict(predicate, judged=None):
    """The cardinality this memory ALREADY holds for a relation, or None (W5).

    The first two arms of the precedence `axis_is_multivalued` states -- SEEDED
    before JUDGED -- asked about the RELATION alone, which is what the triage of
    GH #66 needs: the chain that function wants is exactly the page that does not
    fit. The third arm is not here and cannot be: it is LEARNED from a chain and
    has nothing to say about a relation.

    Deliberately a second statement of those two arms rather than a helper the
    other function calls. `axis_is_multivalued` lives inside the chain block that
    `recall` carries byte for byte (the P15 drift lock), and a rule of the NIGHT
    lane may not reach into the read path to be written once. What keeps them
    honest is that both read the same two lists and the same map, in the same
    order, and that a disagreement would show up as a paged enumeration -- which
    `a_relation_this_memory_calls_enumerating_is_never_asked_again` pins.
    """
    key = str(predicate or "")
    if key in CORE_MULTI:
        return "multi"
    if key in CORE_SINGLE:
        return "single"
    verdict = (judged or {}).get(key)
    return verdict if verdict in ("single", "multi") else None


def statement_intent(fact):
    """The intention marker of ONE statement (GH #67).

    `fact_kind` is where the plan/fact distinction lives now that a speech act
    may not be a predicate: a plan about a matter sits on the axis of the matter,
    which is what lets the currency question compare it with the value already
    there. The price of that is exactly this -- the question has to be able to
    tell the two apart, or it would close a fact because somebody INTENDS
    something else. Empty for `world` and `experience`, so an axis carrying no
    plan renders byte for byte the entry it rendered before this package.
    """
    return "planned" if str(fact.get("fact_kind") or "") == "foresight" else ""


def closure_points_backwards(closed):
    """Does this extractor closure point BACKWARDS in time (GH #71)?

    A closure says "this value was replaced", and a replacement carries a
    direction: the statement that ends is the older one. `ended_at` of an
    extraction closure IS the instant the replacing fact started (the lane
    derives it, it never copies it), and `since` is when the statement it ended
    began. So a closure whose end lies BEFORE its own statement was first said
    was written the wrong way round, and no judgement is needed to see it.

    Measured: one of the first three live extractor closures ended a statement
    three days its senior, and the review of that night answered `retract: 0`
    because it was asked about contradicting evidence rather than about
    direction.

    Equality is not inverted. Two statements of one instant have no direction to
    get wrong, and the extraction lane applies that pair for the same reason.
    """
    ended = str(closed.get("ended_at") or "")
    since = str(closed.get("since") or "")
    return bool(ended and since and ended < since)


def axis_pages(rows):
    """The axes carrying a question tonight, and the page of each the judge sees.

    Since W2 nothing across two different values closes anything by itself, so
    this set is exactly what the store cannot decide alone: several statements,
    all open, no invalidation anywhere. Whether they are versions of one changing
    state or an enumeration is a JUDGEMENT (ruling Q2, option B), and the lane
    only ever formulates the question.

    TWO lists come back, and the split is the whole of GH #66:

    * UNDER the page bound -- the entry this lane has offered since W3, unchanged
      to the byte. The judge sees the complete axis, so it can answer about it.
    * OVER it -- an axis whose open statements do not fit one page. Until #66
      such an axis was dropped right here, and on the track-end corpus that
      silently removed 39 percent of all multi-statement axes (72 of 185) from
      the round: precisely the bucket axes the currency question was opened for.
      The reason for the drop stands and is not weakened -- a judge shown six of
      seventy plans cannot tell it is looking at a bucket, so a truncated page
      would be worse than none. What changes is that the axis leaves here as a
      CANDIDATE carrying the count of what it does not show, and `canon-ask`
      triages it: the cheap question about the RELATION first, a page of the
      currency question only for the relations that answer `single`.

    The bounds, all of them the lesson the axis page taught:

    1. one entry per STATEMENT, never per row. Two assertions of one claim are
       one statement (W2), and the id offered is the assertion still standing:
       the older one is already ended by the arithmetic, so a closure on it would
       collide with a value the chain re-derives every night.
    2. the page of an over-cap axis is its MOST RECENT statements, ordered like
       every other entry, and it says how many statements it leaves behind.
       Recency is what makes the paging sound: closing is the only way to leave
       the open set, so every statement that SURVIVES a page is still among the
       most recent open ones and is on the next page too. The current value is
       carried between pages by that same rule instead of by a second mechanism,
       and no judgement ever compares two statements that were not in one prompt
       together.
    3. busiest axis first, capped -- the same ranking the predicate section uses,
       so one payload stays bounded on a memory that has run for years.

    An axis whose OPEN statements fit but which the extractor closures next to
    them push over the bound keeps the behaviour it had: skipped. The page it
    would need is a review page rather than a currency page, and #66 measures
    and claims nothing about it.

    THREE lists come back since GH #71: the closures whose direction is wrong
    are not offered for review at all, they are handed back for the revert. The
    night does not buy an opinion about a closure it is about to take back, and
    it never shows the judge a row whose attribution this same round clears.
    """
    axes, closed_of = {}, {}
    for r in rows:
        if not (subject_key(r) and axis_key(r) and statement_key(r)):
            continue
        key = (str(subject_key(r)), str(axis_key(r)))
        if is_open(r):
            axes.setdefault(key, []).append(r)
        elif str(r.get("closure_source") or "").startswith(CLOSURE_SOURCE_PREFIXES):
            closed_of.setdefault(key, []).append(r)
    under, over, inverted = [], [], []
    for (subject, predicate) in sorted(set(axes) | set(closed_of)):
        chain = axes.get((subject, predicate), [])
        statements = {}
        for r in sorted(chain, key=lambda f: (f.get("valid_from") or "",
                                              f.get("recorded_at") or "",
                                              f.get("id") or "")):
            statements.setdefault(str(statement_key(r)), []).append(r)
        closed = []
        for r in sorted(closed_of.get((subject, predicate), []),
                        key=lambda f: (f.get("valid_from") or "", f.get("id") or "")):
            item = {"id": str(r.get("id") or ""), "claim": str(r.get("claim") or ""),
                    "since": str(r.get("valid_from") or ""),
                    "ended_at": str(r.get("expired_at") or ""),
                    "closed_by": str(r.get("closure_source") or "")}
            # GH #71: the one property of a closure this lane can check without a
            # model. The reason is the two instants themselves -- a retraction
            # nobody can read back cannot be reverted either (ruling Q2 rail 2).
            if closure_points_backwards(item):
                inverted.append({"id": item["id"], "subject": subject,
                                 "predicate": predicate, "closed_by": item["closed_by"],
                                 "reason": "direction: the statement holds since "
                                           + item["since"] + " and was ended at "
                                           + item["ended_at"] + ", by a fact older "
                                           "than itself"})
                continue
            closed.append(item)
        # A single open statement with nothing closed next to it has no question
        # left; one WITH a recent extract closure has the only question this half
        # of W4 exists for, and W3's rule would never have looked at that axis
        # again.
        if len(statements) < 2 and not closed:
            continue
        items = []
        for a in statements.values():
            item = {"id": str(a[-1].get("id") or ""), "claim": str(a[-1].get("claim") or ""),
                    "since": str(a[0].get("valid_from") or ""),
                    "last_asserted": str(a[-1].get("valid_from") or ""),
                    "assertions": len(a)}
            # GH #67, and present only when it says something: the statement
            # still standing decides, because that is the assertion the judge is
            # shown and the one a closure would name.
            intent = statement_intent(a[-1])
            if intent:
                item["intent"] = intent
            items.append(item)
        items.sort(key=lambda s: (s["since"], s["last_asserted"], s["id"]))
        entry = {"subject": subject, "predicate": predicate, "statements": items}
        # Present only when something IS closed, so a night on a store the
        # extractor never closed on builds byte for byte the payload W3 built.
        if closed:
            entry["closed"] = closed
        if len(items) + len(closed) <= CANON_MAX_STATEMENTS_PER_AXIS:
            under.append(entry)
            continue
        if len(items) <= CANON_MAX_STATEMENTS_PER_AXIS:
            continue
        entry["statements"] = items[-CANON_MAX_STATEMENTS_PER_AXIS:]
        entry["page"] = {"open_statements": len(items),
                         "shown": len(entry["statements"])}
        if closed:
            entry["closed"] = closed[-CANON_MAX_STATEMENTS_PER_AXIS:]
        over.append(entry)
    under.sort(key=lambda a: (-len(a["statements"]) - len(a.get("closed", [])),
                              a["subject"], a["predicate"]))
    # The candidates are ranked by what they HOLD and not by what they show, so
    # the axis the round is furthest behind on is the one it triages first.
    over.sort(key=lambda a: (-a["page"]["open_statements"], a["subject"], a["predicate"]))
    return under[:CANON_MAX_AXES], over, inverted


def cardinality_candidates(rows):
    """The relations whose CARDINALITY is still an open question (W5, ruling Q3).

    A relation is worth asking about when one of its axes carries more than one
    open statement: that is the only shape where "functional or enumerating"
    changes anything a reader sees. Two conditions take a predicate out of the
    list, and both are precedence rather than economy:

    1. SEEDED. The curated list is the authority (ruling Q3), so a predicate on
       either half of it is not a question -- and a judged row for it must never
       exist, or the reader would have to untangle a precedence the data itself
       contradicts.
    2. ALREADY JUDGED -- applied one phase later, at `canon-ask`, where the
       parked verdict map is in hand. The scan proposes, the ask cuts to the
       budget once it knows what is already decided; the same division of labour
       the entity feed has, where the index proposes and the round cuts.

    Ranked by the busiest axis, because that is where an enumeration hides, and
    the tie-break is the name so that two runs over one store build one payload.
    """
    per_axis, values = {}, {}
    for r in rows:
        if not is_open(r) or not axis_key(r) or not subject_key(r) or not statement_key(r):
            continue
        predicate = str(axis_key(r))
        if predicate in CORE_MULTI or predicate in CORE_SINGLE:
            continue
        per_axis.setdefault(predicate, {}).setdefault(
            str(subject_key(r)), set()).add(str(statement_key(r)))
        claim = str(r.get("claim") or "")
        if claim:
            values.setdefault(predicate, set()).add(claim)
    out = []
    for predicate, axes in per_axis.items():
        busiest = max(len(s) for s in axes.values())
        if busiest < 2:
            continue
        out.append({"predicate": predicate,
                    "values": sorted(values.get(predicate, set()))[:CANON_MAX_CARD_VALUES],
                    "open_statements": busiest})
    out.sort(key=lambda c: (-c["open_statements"], c["predicate"]))
    return [{"predicate": c["predicate"], "values": c["values"]}
            for c in out[:CANON_MAX_PREDICATES]]


def sup_scope_op():
    """Ask which axes are live -- the entry of the supersession arithmetic (R9).

    A helper rather than an inline literal because three phases reach it now: the
    belief apply (with the canonicalisation round switched off), the end of that
    round, and its error path. All three have to enter the arithmetic through the
    SAME door, or a run would materialise different spans depending on which way
    it came in.
    """
    return store_op({"operation": "select", "table": "facts",
                     "columns": ["id", "subject", "canonical_subject", "canonical_predicate"],
                     "where": {"expired_at": {"is_null": True}}}, "sup-scope")


# ----------------------------------------------- the questions of ONE night (#69)
# The round stays ONE call carrying every question the night has -- that half is
# deliberate. What is not deliberate, and what GH #69 removes, is describing a
# question whose data section is empty: the payload builder has left such a
# section out since W5, the instructions were rendered whole regardless, so a
# store with nothing to canonicalise still bought the entire block every night.
#
# Three rules keep the shrinking honest:
#
# 1. A section renders when its DATA section carries something, and the ANSWER
#    SHAPE shrinks with it. The judge is never asked for a key it has no question
#    for, and never left with a question whose key it may not use.
# 2. A constraint lives with the question whose ANSWERS it guards -- "do not
#    merge two quantities" with the rewordings, "do not close an enumeration"
#    with the currency question, "names are verbatim" with the entity pairs. The
#    two questions that could constrain each other across the boundary hang on
#    the SAME data section (`axes` carries both 3 and 5), so they are never
#    rendered apart. The one genuinely shared block is the core vocabulary, and
#    it belongs to question 1: the cardinality question never sees a seeded
#    relation, `cardinality_candidates` drops those before the payload exists.
# 3. The numbering is FIXED. A question is `3.` on every night it is asked and is
#    never renumbered, so a shrunken block and the full one describe the same
#    five questions and no cross reference between them can go stale.
#
# A night that carries all five sections renders BYTE FOR BYTE what it rendered
# before this change -- that is what lets the verdicts of a full night be pinned
# without buying a model.
CANON_COUNT_WORDS = {1: "One", 2: "Two", 3: "Three", 4: "Four", 5: "Five"}


def canon_questions(inventory, pairs, axes, cardinality):
    """The data sections one night carries, one name per question group (#69).

    `predicates` needs TWO relations for the reason the round has always skipped
    the call over one: a single relation cannot be a synonym of itself. The other
    three are simply there or not there.

    `paged` (GH #66) is the one name that is not a section of its own: it is a
    SHAPE the axis section can be in, it declares no answer key, and it can never
    stand without `axes`. It obeys the same rule as the four -- the paragraph
    describing a page is rendered on the nights that carry one, and on no other.
    """
    present = set()
    if len(inventory) >= 2:
        present.add("predicates")
    if pairs:
        present.add("entity_pairs")
    if axes:
        present.add("axes")
        # GH #66: an axis that arrives as a PAGE brings one paragraph with it and
        # no new answer key. It is judged with the same three answers as any
        # other axis; what it needs said is that it IS a page, which is the one
        # thing the judge cannot see from a list of six statements.
        if any(isinstance(a, dict) and isinstance(a.get("page"), dict) for a in axes):
            present.add("paged")
    if cardinality:
        present.add("cardinality")
    return present


def canon_shape(present):
    """The declared answer shape, one fragment per question that is asked."""
    out = []
    if "predicates" in present:
        out.append("\"predicates\":[{\"alias\":\"\",\"canonical\":\"\"}]")
    if "entity_pairs" in present:
        out.append("\"entities\":[{\"alias\":\"\",\"canonical\":\"\"}]")
    # The refusal log is fed by TWO questions -- the entity pairs of 2 and the
    # rewordings of 5 -- so it stands while either is asked. The dimension shown
    # is the one this night can actually receive: an item that names none is read
    # as `subject` on the apply side, so a night without entity pairs shows the
    # claim dimension instead of inviting a refusal on a question nobody asked.
    if "entity_pairs" in present or "axes" in present:
        out.append("\"different\":[{\"dimension\":\"%s\",\"left\":\"\",\"right\":\"\"}]"
                   % ("subject" if "entity_pairs" in present else "claim"))
    if "axes" in present:
        out.append("\"closures\":[{\"subject\":\"\",\"predicate\":\"\",\"closed\":\"\","
                   "\"superseded_by\":\"\",\"ended_at\":\"\",\"reason\":\"\"}]")
        out.append("\"reopenings\":[{\"subject\":\"\",\"predicate\":\"\",\"statement\":\"\","
                   "\"closed_by\":\"\",\"reason\":\"\"}]")
    if "cardinality" in present:
        out.append("\"cardinality\":[{\"predicate\":\"\",\"verdict\":\"\",\"reason\":\"\"}]")
    if "axes" in present:
        out.append("\"same_value\":[{\"subject\":\"\",\"predicate\":\"\",\"canonical\":\"\","
                   "\"alias\":\"\",\"reason\":\"\"}]")
    return "{" + ",".join(out) + "}"


def canon_overview(present):
    """The map of the questions, written for the questions that are there.

    The ordinals are the FIXED numbers, never positions in the rendered block:
    "the third" is question 3 whether or not 1 and 2 were asked tonight.
    """
    asked = len([q for q in ("predicates", "entity_pairs", "cardinality") if q in present])
    if "axes" in present:
        asked += 2
    if asked >= 5:
        out = ["Five questions in one payload."]
    else:
        out = ["%s of the five questions in one payload -- the numbering is fixed, and a "
               "question this payload does not carry is not asked tonight."
               % CANON_COUNT_WORDS.get(asked, "None")]
    identity = " about IDENTITY: nothing you say there changes a stored value, it states that " \
               "two spellings are one thing."
    if "predicates" in present and "entity_pairs" in present:
        out.append("The first two are" + identity)
    elif "predicates" in present:
        out.append("The first is" + identity)
    elif "entity_pairs" in present:
        out.append("The second is" + identity)
    if "axes" in present:
        out.append("The third is about CURRENCY: which of the statements this memory holds are "
                   "still true.")
    if "cardinality" in present:
        out.append("The fourth is about the SHAPE of a relation and is answered once per "
                   "relation, not per value.")
    out.append("None of your answers ever deletes a row or edits a written value.")
    return " ".join(out)

def canon_instructions(present):
    """The instruction block of ONE night: the questions it has data for (#69).

    Question 3 and question 5 read the same `axes` section with two different
    questions, so they render together or not at all -- which is why neither of
    the constraints they put on each other can ever be dropped alone.
    """
    out = ["You are the judge of an agent's memory. Answer with JSON only, no prose, shape: ",
           canon_shape(present), ".\n\n", canon_overview(present), "\n\n"]
    if "predicates" in present:
        out.append(CANON_PREDICATES_Q)
    if "entity_pairs" in present:
        out.append(CANON_ENTITIES_Q)
    if "axes" in present:
        out.append(CANON_CURRENCY_Q)
        # GH #66: between the two questions that read the axis page, because it
        # constrains the first and is read by the second.
        if "paged" in present:
            out.append(CANON_PAGED_Q)
        out.append(CANON_REWORDING_Q)
    if "cardinality" in present:
        out.append(CANON_CARDINALITY_Q)
    out.append(CANON_CLOSING)
    return "".join(out)


def derived_audience(source_ids, fact_audience):
    """The audience of DERIVED knowledge: the INTERSECTION of its sources'.

    A belief rests on facts. It may only be told to whoever could have heard
    EVERY one of them; anything wider is a laundry, where two private facts go
    in and one shareable claim comes out (#244, contract Nachtrag 1).

    Three cases that are decisions rather than accidents:

      * An EMPTY intersection is a legitimate result -- the belief is then
        visible to nobody. It is not widened to ["*"] and not resolved into a
        union: a belief no round may hear is a belief waiting for a round that
        may, and the alternative is the leak this column exists to close.
      * "*" in a source is NEUTRAL: universal cuts nothing away.
      * A source that is missing, or that carries no audience_set, contributes
        the EMPTY set, not "don't care". An untagged fact is invisible, and
        nothing derived from it may be more visible than it is.
    """
    ids = [str(x) for x in (source_ids or [])]
    if not ids:
        return json.dumps([])
    acc = None
    for fid in ids:
        raw = fact_audience.get(fid)
        try:
            items = json.loads(raw) if raw else []
        except Exception:
            items = []
        if not isinstance(items, list):
            items = []
        cur = {str(x) for x in items if str(x)}
        if cur == {"*"}:
            continue
        acc = cur if acc is None else (acc & cur)
        if not acc:
            break
    if acc is None:
        # every source was universal, so the intersection is too
        return json.dumps(["*"])
    return json.dumps(sorted(acc))


def read_verdict_scratch():
    """Read the verdict and the known-belief ids back under one key. The store
    has no joins, so both halves meet in `scratch` before the apply phase."""
    return store_op({"operation": "select", "table": "scratch",
                     "columns": ["key", "kind", "payload"], "where": {"key": run_id}},
                    "apply-run")


def call_receipt(caller):
    """The token receipt of ONE model call, read off the hop of the reply that
    carried it (GH #64). The two field names are the ones the llm cells emit and
    the ones the embedding lane adopted in GH #9, so the books of a night and the
    message log count the same thing. A reply without a usage block books the
    CALL and no tokens: a zero would read as a call that was free, and nothing
    downstream could tell those two apart again."""
    receipt = {"call": caller}
    for field in ("tokens_prompt", "tokens_completion"):
        value = hop.get(field)
        if isinstance(value, int) and not isinstance(value, bool):
            receipt[field] = value
    return receipt


def park_call(caller):
    """Park that receipt under the run key. A run closes several store round
    trips after the model answered, where this hop is long gone -- so a call
    meets its own books the way every other artefact of this lane does. ONE row
    per call and never an updated counter: a crashed night that is re-run then
    books what it really cost instead of what one pass costs."""
    return store_op({"operation": "insert", "table": "scratch",
                     "row": {"key": run_id, "kind": "llm-call", "created_at": delta_to,
                             "payload": json.dumps(call_receipt(caller), sort_keys=True)}},
                    "llm-call")


def park_pages(coverage):
    """Park what the night did with the axes one page cannot hold (GH #66).

    Written by the ASK, because the ASK is where the triage happens, and read
    back into the run receipt by `apply-run` like every other artefact of this
    lane. That it does not wait for the answer is the point: which axes were put
    in front of the judge, and which were answered for good without asking, is a
    fact about the NIGHT and not about the reply -- so a night whose judge never
    answered still receipts its coverage.
    """
    return store_op({"operation": "insert", "table": "scratch",
                     "row": {"key": run_id, "kind": "canon-pages", "created_at": delta_to,
                             "payload": json.dumps(coverage, sort_keys=True)}},
                    "canon-pages")


def close_run(llm_calls, verdicts_json, receipts=()):
    """Close the books of the run. `llm_calls` counts the model calls of the
    night -- since GH #64 the canonicalisation judge is one of them and not an
    invisible second bill. The token columns are SUMS over those same calls and
    are written only when at least one reply reported usage: left out they stay
    NULL, which reads as "nobody reported" instead of "nothing was spent"."""
    booked = {"status": "done", "finished_at": delta_to,
              "llm_calls": llm_calls, "verdicts": verdicts_json}
    for field in ("tokens_prompt", "tokens_completion"):
        known = [r.get(field) for r in receipts
                 if isinstance(r.get(field), int) and not isinstance(r.get(field), bool)]
        if known:
            booked[field] = sum(known)
    return store_op({"operation": "update", "table": "consolidation_log",
                     "set": booked, "where": {"run_id": run_id}}, "closed")

#

# facts_in_window: 0` -- and every later night derives `delta_from` from the
# newest done row, so the window nothing ever looked at is skipped forever. That

# that carries no run identity -- correct for a stray echo, wrong for a refusal:
